## <mark>ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS</mark>

<mark>Advances are taking place in understanding the pathogenesis of acanthosis nigricans.</mark> <mark>Insulin clearly plays a central role in the presentation of acanthosis nigricans.</mark> In a subset of women with hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance with acanthosis nigricans, loss of function mutations in the insulin receptor or anti-insulin receptor antibodies can be found (Type A and Type B insulin resistance syndromes). <mark>It is postulated that excess growth factor stimulation in the skin causes the aberrant proliferation of keratinocytes and fibroblasts, resulting in the characteristic phenotype of acanthosis nigricans.</mark> <mark>In states of insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia, acanthosis nigricans may result from excess insulin binding to IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts.</mark> IGF-1 receptors are expressed on basal keratinocytes and are upregulated in proliferative skin conditions.

<mark>Studies show that high concentrations of insulin stimulate fibroblast proliferation through IGF-1 receptors in vitro.</mark> <mark>Other members of the tyrosine kinase receptor family, including the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR), have also been implicated in acanthosis nigricans.</mark> Several genetic syndromes—such as Crouzon syndrome and SADDAN (severe achondroplasia with developmental delay and acanthosis nigricans)—are caused by mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) and result in acanthosis nigricans in the absence of hyperinsulinemia or obesity, implicating this growth factor receptor in the disease’s pathogenesis. In cases of malignant acanthosis nigricans, transforming growth factor-α (TGF-α) released by tumor cells may stimulate keratinocyte proliferation via activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor.

Support for the role of various growth factors in the pathogenesis of acanthosis nigricans continues to grow.

<mark>In addition to direct effects of hyperinsulinemia on keratinocytes, insulin also appears to augment androgen levels in women.</mark> <mark>High insulin levels stimulate ovarian androgen production and can lead to ovarian hypertrophy with cystic changes.</mark> <mark>Although acanthosis nigricans is commonly associated with elevated androgens in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), the skin lesions do not reliably respond to antiandrogen therapy, suggesting that hyperinsulinemia plays a more central role than hyperandrogenism in lesion development.</mark> <mark>Several drugs have also been reported to cause acanthosis nigricans, including systemic glucocorticoids, nicotinic acid, and estrogens such as diethylstilbestrol.</mark>

## <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS: CUTANEOUS LESIONS</mark>

<mark>Clinically, acanthosis nigricans presents as brown to gray-black, papillomatous, hyperpigmented skin thickening in flexural areas, most commonly the posterolateral neck, axillae, groin, and abdominal folds.</mark> <mark>The distribution is typically symmetric.</mark> <mark>Affected skin has a velvety, "dirty" appearance.</mark> 

<mark>The back of the neck is the most consistently and severely affected site.</mark> <mark>Superimposed acrochordons (skin tags) frequently develop in involved areas.</mark> <mark>In more severe or florid cases, involvement may extend to the dorsal hands, knuckles, and even the palms, where a rugated (ridged) pattern may be observed.</mark>

<mark>Mucosal surfaces—including oral, esophageal, pharyngeal, laryngeal, conjunctival, and anogenital regions—can also be involved, though this is less common.</mark>

# Paraneoplastic Dermatoses

There is an evolving consensus regarding what constitutes a true paraneoplastic syndrome. Two essential criteria must be met:  
1. The dermatosis must develop after the onset of the malignant tumor, even if the tumor is asymptomatic or occult.  
2. The dermatosis and the malignancy must follow a parallel course—complete removal of the tumor leads to resolution of the skin condition, and tumor recurrence results in relapse of the dermatosis.  

A classification of clinicopathologic categories is outlined in Table 154-1.

## Epidemiology

Skin changes can serve as markers of internal malignancy, although the exact prevalence is unknown due to variability in disease presentation and the rarity of certain conditions. The risk of developing a paraneoplastic dermatosis correlates with age, sex, and established risk factors for the associated internal malignancy.

The strength of the association between a specific dermatosis and cancer varies. For example, **hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita** is linked to a broad range of malignancies, whereas **necrolytic migratory erythema (NME)** is highly specific for glucagon-producing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. Specific malignancy associations for each paraneoplastic dermatosis are detailed in Table 154-1.

## Etiology and Pathogenesis

Paraneoplastic dermatoses are classified by their primary clinical features. A more precise pathophysiologic classification is limited by incomplete understanding of underlying mechanisms.

Establishing a definitive link between a cutaneous eruption and an internal malignancy is easier when both the skin condition and the tumor are rare. Challenges arise when the dermatosis is common—such as **seborrheic keratoses** in **Leser-Trélat sign**—and is associated with a wide range of frequently occurring cancers, leading to numerous anecdotal reports.

## <mark>Hyperkeratotic Dermatoses</mark>

### <mark>Acanthosis Nigricans (See Chap. 152)</mark>

<mark>The term *acanthosis nigricans* was introduced by Unna, though the first cases linked to malignancy were described independently by Pollitzer and Janovsky in 1890.</mark> <mark>Curth classified acanthosis nigricans into malignant, benign, syndromic, and pseudoacanthosis nigricans (associated with obesity).</mark>

### <mark>Epidemiology</mark>

<mark>Approximately 80% of acanthosis nigricans cases are idiopathic or associated with benign conditions such as endocrinopathies or hereditary disorders.</mark> <mark>Malignancy-associated acanthosis nigricans is rare, occurring in 1 of 35 patients with intrathoracic or intra-abdominal malignancies and in 2 of 12,000 cancer patients overall.</mark> <mark>It predominantly affects individuals over 40 years of age, with at least 80% of malignant cases occurring in this group.</mark>

## Paraneoplastic Dermatoses: At a Glance

Skin manifestations can signal internal malignancy through:
- Epi-phenomenon  
- Familial cancer syndromes  
- Direct tumor extension  

**Key Features of Paraneoplastic Dermatoses:**
- Follow a parallel course with the underlying malignancy  
- Enable early diagnosis and disease monitoring  

**Dermatoses strongly associated with internal malignancy:**
- Tripe palms  
- Bazex syndrome  
- Paraneoplastic pemphigus  
- Erythema gyratum repens  
- Necrolytic migratory erythema  
- Hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita  

**Dermatoses weakly associated with internal malignancy:**
- Acanthosis nigricans  
- Acquired ichthyosis  
- Multiple seborrheic keratoses  

**Management:** Treatment of the dermatosis centers on identifying and managing the underlying malignancy.

# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS: CUTANEOUS LESIONS</mark>

The clinical presentation of Cushing syndrome may be subtle. <mark>Skin findings are often present, and when carefully correlated with systemic complaints, they can lead to an early diagnosis.</mark> Common skin manifestations include easy bruisability and skin thinning. Mild hypertrichosis, typically of the lanugo type, and acne may also occur. Frank hirsutism and severe acne suggest the possibility of a concurrent androgen-secreting tumor.

The development of multiple violaceous striae wider than $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ on the abdomen or proximal extremities is highly suggestive of Cushing syndrome. The width and violaceous color of these striae help differentiate them from the narrower, hypopigmented striae commonly seen in pregnancy or with rapid weight gain.

<mark>Relatively dramatic changes in fat distribution often accompany generalized weight gain.</mark> There is increased central adiposity with thinning of the extremities. Central obesity, along with facial fat accumulation, leads to a rounded facial appearance known as **moon facies**, often accompanied by facial erythema and telangiectasias. Additional fat deposition occurs in the dorsocervical region (buffalo hump) and supraclavicular fossae. Men may develop **gynecomastia**.

<mark>Although uncommon, **hyperpigmentation** can occur in Cushing syndrome, particularly when there is marked overproduction of ACTH—most often from an ectopic source, but sometimes from the pituitary.</mark> <mark>Both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC), contribute to increased melanin production, similar to what is seen in Addison disease.</mark>

<mark>**Acanthosis nigricans** may be present due to insulin resistance associated with Cushing syndrome, which often leads to diabetes mellitus.</mark> The immunosuppressive effects of excess glucocorticoids predispose patients to increased **dermatophyte and candidal infections** of the skin and nails.

<mark>Women may present with **irregular menses or amenorrhea**.</mark> Other systemic features include **hypertension, osteoporosis, muscle wasting, and proximal muscle weakness**.

# LABORATORY TESTS

Diagnostic confirmation of Cushing syndrome requires demonstration of excess cortisol production. Cortisol levels exhibit diurnal variation, typically peaking in the early morning. Therefore, serum cortisol should be measured at 8 A.M.

The average daily cortisol production can be assessed via **24-hour urinary free cortisol** measurement. Any abnormal result should be confirmed with repeat testing (two to three times).

If urinary or serum cortisol levels are elevated, the diagnosis is supported by **failure to suppress** cortisol during a **low-dose dexamethasone suppression test** (e.g., 1 mg overnight or 2 mg over 48 hours).

Further testing, such as the **high-dose dexamethasone suppression test**, helps differentiate pituitary-dependent Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH production or adrenal tumors.

It is important to note that **hypercortisolism** can be present in the absence of true Cushing syndrome (e.g., in pseudo-Cushing states such as obesity, depression, or alcoholism), so careful clinical correlation is essential.

## Treatment of Unwanted Hair Growth

<mark>The use of anti-androgens may help reduce hair growth, but monotherapy is unlikely to eliminate it completely (Box 86-3).</mark> Temporary hair removal methods such as shaving, plucking, and depilatory creams can be irritating and painful. <mark>Topical eflornithine 13.9%—an inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase—is approved for reducing unwanted facial hair in women when applied twice daily.</mark>

Laser epilation is less permanent than commonly believed and works best with repeated treatments. Patients should be counseled against unrealistic expectations. The mechanism involves selective photothermolysis, where melanin in the hair shaft absorbs light energy, leading to targeted destruction of hair follicles. Combining topical eflornithine with laser therapy may enhance outcomes by slowing regrowth after hair removal.

Weight loss can be beneficial in obese individuals, as obesity lowers sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) levels, increasing free testosterone, and contributes to insulin resistance, both of which can exacerbate hirsutism.

Systemic treatments show marginal differences in efficacy, but all typically require 6 to 12 months to achieve clinically significant miniaturization of terminal hairs. Options include:
- **Oral anti-androgens** such as spironolactone (100–200 mg daily) or cyproterone acetate
- **Oral contraceptives**, which suppress androgen synthesis by reducing gonadotropin secretion; they are most effective when combined with anti-androgens
- **Finasteride**, a 5α-reductase inhibitor

In cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, low-dose dexamethasone can be used to suppress adrenal androgen overproduction. Hyperprolactinemia may be managed medically (e.g., bromocriptine) or surgically, depending on the cause, and may also require adjunctive anti-androgen therapy.

## Hypertrichosis

### Congenital Hypertrichosis Lanuginosa

Congenital hypertrichosis lanuginosa is characterized by a generalized, confluent overgrowth of fine, silvery blonde to gray lanugo hair present at birth or in early infancy. It is extremely rare (approximately 1 in 1 billion) and typically follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with variable expressivity. Most affected children are otherwise healthy, although dental anomalies may occur. The hair distribution may persist, increase, or regress with age.

### Other Congenital Disorders with Hypertrichosis

Other congenital conditions associated with generalized hypertrichosis exist, but none exhibit the uniform distribution seen in congenital hypertrichosis lanuginosa (Table 86-10). These include:

- **Ambras syndrome (hypertrichosis universalis congenita)**: Autosomal dominant condition featuring long, thick hair, especially on the face, ears, and shoulders. It is often accompanied by facial dysmorphism and dental abnormalities.
- **X-linked dominant congenital generalized hypertrichosis**: Seen in a five-generation family, with more pronounced terminal hair on the face and upper body, particularly in males.
- **Gingival fibromatosis with hypertrichosis**: Autosomal dominant (rarely recessive) disorder associated with hypertrichosis of the face, eyebrows, limbs, and upper back, along with seizures and intellectual disability (oligophrenia). Hypertrichosis may appear at puberty, while gingival overgrowth typically emerges with primary tooth eruption.

## <mark>Acquired Generalized Hypertrichosis</mark>

The sudden onset of generalized hypertrichosis without an identifiable drug trigger is a concerning clinical sign. Acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa is strongly associated with underlying malignancy and may precede the diagnosis of cancer. It should prompt a thorough systemic evaluation for occult neoplasm (Fig. 86-29; see also eFig. 86-29.1 in online edition; Table 86-10; Chap. [reference incomplete]).

# GENERALIZED HYPERTRICHOSIS

There are several drugs that routinely cause generalized hypertrichosis. <mark>Oral minoxidil, a piperidinopyrimidine derivative and potassium channel opener used as a systemic antihypertensive agent, causes hypertrichosis in 80% of patients, most prominently on the face, shoulders, and extremities.</mark> <mark>Diazoxide, a benzothiadiazine used in malignant hypertension or idiopathic hypoglycemia of infancy, leads to lanugo-like hypertrichosis of the face, trunk, and extremities in 1% to 20% of adults, but in nearly 100% of children.</mark> <mark>Phenytoin (Dilantin) use results in terminal hair hypertrichosis in 5% to 12% of patients, typically beginning on the extremities, trunk, and face.</mark> <mark>The immunosuppressive immunophilin ligand cyclosporine A causes terminal hair hypertrichosis in 40% to 95% of patients, with a diffuse increase in hair, primarily over the upper body.</mark> <mark>Based on findings in mouse models, the underlying mechanism likely involves premature induction of the anagen phase and inhibition of catagen by cyclosporine A, which may contribute to the conversion of vellus to terminal hair, resulting in hypertrichosis.</mark>

# <mark>TREATMENT</mark>

Removal of the inciting cause should be the primary approach to treatment and usually leads to regression of hypertrichosis. When this is not possible, management focuses on helping the patient cope psychologically with the physical change and/or using temporary or permanent hair removal methods. The same techniques used for hirsutism management can be applied for hypertrichosis, except for anti-androgenic therapies.

## <mark>Other Adverse Effects</mark>

<mark>**Hypertrichosis** occurs in virtually all patients on long-term cyclosporine (CsA) therapy.</mark> <mark>It is not limited to androgen-dependent, hair-bearing areas and does not show a tendency toward spontaneous remission.</mark>  

<mark>**Gingival hypertrophy** is reported in up to 70% of CsA-treated patients and is more common in children, individuals with poor oral hygiene, and those concomitantly using calcium channel blockers.</mark> <mark>Improvement in gingival overgrowth has been observed with topical or systemic azithromycin and metronidazole.</mark>  

<mark>An **acneiform eruption**, clinically indistinguishable from steroid-induced acne, is frequently reported.</mark> <mark>A disseminated comedonal or cystic acneiform eruption may also occur.</mark> <mark>These dermatologic side effects can appear at any time during CsA therapy, though they are most commonly observed at treatment initiation.</mark>  

<mark>Other cutaneous manifestations include **keratosis pilaris**, **sebaceous hyperplasia**, **warts**, and **epidermal inclusion cysts**, which occur in up to one-third of CsA-treated patients.</mark>

<mark>**Osteoporosis** may result from CsA’s effects on osteoblasts and osteoclasts, as well as alterations in lymphokine release.</mark>  

<mark>CsA can induce **hyperuricemia** in up to 15% of patients, which may also serve as an early indicator of CsA-induced nephrotoxicity.</mark>  

<mark>**Myopathy** has been reported in transplant patients receiving high doses of CsA.</mark> <mark>Caution is advised when combining CsA with statins due to an increased risk of myotoxicity.</mark>

## Pregnancy

CsA does not appear to be mutagenic or teratogenic. However, in pregnant women taking CsA—particularly transplant recipients—there is an increased incidence of **preterm birth**, **fetal growth retardation**, **abortion**, **preeclampsia**, and **hypertension**. These risks are heightened in transplant patients.  

No neonatal complications have been reported in children born to fathers receiving CsA.  

CsA crosses the placenta and is excreted in breast milk. Therefore, **adequate contraception** is recommended for women of childbearing potential.  

CsA-treated transplant patients have a lower relative risk of life-threatening infectious complications compared to those receiving azathioprine and prednisolone. Nonetheless, **increased vigilance for infections** is warranted in all CsA-treated patients.

## Tacrolimus (TCL)

Tacrolimus (TCL), a calcineurin inhibitor formerly known as FK506, is a macrolactam drug initially isolated from *Streptomyces tsukubaensis*.

### Mechanism of Action

The proposed mechanisms of action of TCL are similar, if not identical, to those of CsA (see Macrolactam Drugs).

### Pharmacokinetics

TCL can be administered **orally**, **topically**, and **intravenously**. Systemic pharmacokinetics follow a two-compartment model, characterized by a rapid initial distribution phase and a terminal elimination half-life of 12 to 21 hours. TCL is primarily metabolized in the liver, with less than 1% excreted unchanged in urine.

While TCL has not been shown to be more effective than CsA, it demonstrates **better bioavailability**. Topical formulations are available as 0.3% and 0.1% ointments; for additional details, refer to Chapter 221.

### Dosing Regimen

|          | ORAL               | INTRAVENOUS         |
|----------|--------------------|---------------------|
| Adults   | 150–200 μg/kg/day  | 25–50 μg/kg/day     |
| Children | 200–300 μg/kg/day  | 50–100 μg/kg/day    |

### Initiating Therapy

In patients with hepatic dysfunction, the systemic TCL dose should be reduced by 10% to 30% from the standard regimen.

### Monitoring Therapy

Whole blood concentrations of TCL can be reliably monitored using either **enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)** or **HPLC mass spectrometry**, with good correlation between the two methods.

## <mark>Bacillary Angiomatosis (BA)</mark>

Currently, the prevalence of bacillary angiomatosis (BA) in North America and Western Europe is very low, primarily due to improved immune function in HIV-infected patients on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and the use of prophylactic treatments against organisms such as *Mycobacterium avium complex* (MAC).

<mark>Clinically, the cutaneous lesions of BA are red to violaceous, dome-shaped papules, nodules, or plaques that resemble Kaposi sarcoma or pyogenic granuloma.</mark> <mark>These lesions range in size from a few millimeters to 2–3 cm in diameter and represent dermal vascular proliferations with overlying thinned or eroded epidermis.</mark> Less commonly, dome-shaped subcutaneous masses may occur without the characteristic red color seen in more superficial vascular lesions.

Lesions are typically soft to firm and may be tender on palpation. <mark>The number of lesions varies widely—from a single lesion to more than 100, and in rare cases, exceeding 1000.</mark> Nearly any cutaneous site can be involved, although the palms, soles, and oral cavity are usually spared.

Following hematogenous or lymphatic dissemination, *Bartonella henselae* and *Bartonella quintana* can cause systemic disease, including soft-tissue masses, bone marrow involvement, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly. Internal organ involvement may occur with or without concurrent cutaneous lesions.

The clinical course of BA is variable. In some patients, lesions regress spontaneously. However, as with other opportunistic infections in HIV, BA may recur, especially in the setting of persistent immunosuppression.

### Treatment
The antibiotics of choice for BA are:
- **Erythromycin**: 250–500 mg orally four times daily
- **Doxycycline**: 100 mg orally twice daily

Treatment should continue until complete resolution of lesions, which typically takes 3 to 4 weeks. Alternative effective agents include rifampin, ciprofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), particularly for patients intolerant to first-line therapies.

Secondary prophylaxis is recommended for patients with recurrent BA.

## Fungal Infections

Cutaneous fungal infections in HIV disease manifest as:
- Superficial infections (dermatomycoses)
- Invasive cutaneous infections
- Systemic fungal infections with hematogenous spread to the skin

Superficial pathogens such as *Trichosporon beigelii* can disseminate as immune function declines. Dissemination may present atypically; for example, *Trichophyton rubrum* has been reported to disseminate and clinically mimic Kaposi sarcoma.

The widespread use of HAART has significantly reduced the incidence of these infections. Additionally, drug interactions between HAART and antifungal agents appear to be less clinically significant than previously believed.

### Dermatophytoses

*Trichophyton rubrum* is the most common cause of **proximal subungual onychomycosis**, an infection involving the undersurface of the proximal nail plate. This condition is strongly associated with HIV infection and should prompt consideration of HIV testing.

In advanced HIV disease, epidermal dermatophytosis can be extensive, persistent, and recurrent. Without restoration of immune function, these infections tend to be chronic.

### Mucocutaneous Candidiasis

Cutaneous *Candida* infections such as intertrigo are relatively uncommon in HIV-infected adults, though the prevalence may increase in those with HAART-associated diabetes mellitus.

*Candida* infections frequently affect moist, keratinized areas such as the anogenital region. **Angular cheilitis**, characterized by inflammation at the corners of the mouth, may occur unilaterally or bilaterally. It can appear in isolation or in conjunction with oropharyngeal or esophageal candidiasis.

In HIV-infected children, common presentations include:
- Diaper-area candidiasis
- Intertrigo in the axillae and neck folds
- Chronic *Candida* paronychia of the fingernails, often leading to secondary nail dystrophy (onychia)

### Oropharyngeal Candidiasis

*Candida* colonization of the oropharynx is common in HIV-infected individuals, often occurring in the absence of symptoms. Its presence may warrant HIV testing.

- *C. albicans* is the most frequently isolated species.
- Colonization with non-*albicans* species alone is associated with advanced HIV disease and very low CD4+ T-cell counts.

Oropharyngeal candidiasis serves as a clinical marker of HIV disease progression.

# Dermoscopy and In Vivo Imaging

Dermoscopy is more sensitive than visual inspection in detecting orifices, vessels, and specific vascular patterns such as crown, radial, flower, and punctiform arrangements.

In vivo confocal microscopy reveals a round, well-circumscribed lesion with central cystic areas filled with brightly refractile material, corresponding to molluscum bodies seen on histopathology.

# <mark>Laboratory</mark>

Laboratory testing is not routinely required for the diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum, as clinical and dermoscopic evaluation is typically sufficient.

In uncertain cases, confirmation can be achieved through histological examination, polymerase chain reaction, or electron microscopy. Histology shows the characteristic "nuts in a sack" pattern. Electron microscopy identifies the brick-shaped virions of molluscum contagiosum virus.

# Histopathology

Haematoxylin and eosin staining of molluscum contagiosum lesions typically shows a crateriform, hyperplastic epidermis or endophytic infundibular hyperplasia, forming a circumscribed cup-shaped pseudotumor. This structure contains large cells with granular, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies (also known as inclusion bodies or Henderson-Paterson bodies). These inclusion bodies can measure up to 35 microns in diameter and consist of millions of virions that compress the keratinocyte nuclei. They progressively enlarge and become basophilic before being released onto the skin surface.

Unusual histological variants include pseudocystic, giant, and pedunculated forms. Disseminated, confluent, or atypical giant lesions may indicate immunosuppression, particularly HIV infection.

Special stains such as Lendrum's phloxine tartrazine or toluidine blue/Giemsa are rarely needed, as inclusion bodies are usually evident on routine staining. However, these stains may be helpful when folliculitis, abscess formation following follicular rupture, or a dense inflammatory infiltrate obscure the inclusions.

Occasionally, a dense dermal lymphocytic infiltrate with CD30-positive cells may mimic anaplastic large cell lymphoma or lymphomatoid papulosis. Molluscum bodies can be identified by immunohistochemistry on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue, and cross-reactivity with Melan A—a melanocytic marker—has been reported.

Immunohistochemical studies are reserved for research and not used in routine diagnosis. Additional histological findings may include perilesional fibro-oedematous to fibromyxoid stroma, and rarely amyloid-like deposits, anetoderma, or metaplastic ossification. Follicular induction in the adjacent epidermis should not be mistaken for basal cell carcinoma.

In approximately 4% of cases, molluscum contagiosum may coexist with other lesions such as epidermal cysts or melanocytic naevi, potentially masking the characteristic changes. Coinfection with other pathogens—such as human papillomavirus or *Cryptococcus neoformans*—within the same lesion can occur, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

# Differential Diagnosis

Molluscum contagiosum must be differentiated from other conditions, particularly in the setting of possible sexual transmission.

In immunocompetent patients, mimickers include:
- Genital warts (condyloma acuminata)
- Flat warts
- Lichen planus
- Lichen nitidus
- Condylomata lata of secondary syphilis
- Pyogenic granuloma
- Ectopic sebaceous glands
- Dermal cyst
- Vulvar lymphangioma circumscriptum
- Keratoacanthoma
- Basal cell carcinoma
- Amelanotic melanoma

In immunosuppressed patients, opportunistic infections that may resemble molluscum contagiosum include:
- *Penicillium marneffei* (penicilliosis)
- *Cryptococcus neoformans* (cryptococcosis)
- *Coccidioides* spp. (coccidioidomycosis)
- *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis*
- *Aspergillus fumigatus* (aspergillosis)
- *Sporothrix schenckii*
